Clinical Reference

Infective Endocarditis

On this page
Microbial infection of the endocardial surface, whose lesion — the vegetation — is an avascular platelet–fibrin biofilm that neutrophils cannot enter and antibiotics barely penetrate. That single fact explains the whole disease: bactericidal drugs, high dose, IV, for 4–6 weeks — and a surgeon when the antibiotics cannot win.
S. aureus is now #1 — 31% In-hospital mortality 17–18% Heart failure = #1 surgical indication 3 blood-culture sets BEFORE antibiotics 2023 Duke-ISCVID: 2 major / 1+3 / 5 minor
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

The five-step cascade — how a valve gets infected

Healthy endothelium is essentially non-adhesive to circulating bacteria. You cannot simply seed a normal valve by having bacteria in the blood — if you could, everyone who flosses would get endocarditis. Infective endocarditis (IE) requires a sequence of events, and every step of that sequence is a place where a drug, a procedure, or a surgeon can intervene.

Step 1 — Endothelial injury. Either mechanical damage from turbulent, high-velocity flow (a regurgitant jet, a stenotic orifice, a VSD shunt, a prosthetic sewing ring, a catheter or pacemaker lead rubbing the endocardium), or inflammatory endothelial activation. S. aureus is the exception that proves the rule: it can invade intact endothelium, which is exactly why it is the organism that causes IE on structurally normal valves.

Step 2 — NBTE: the sterile landing pad. Denuded endothelium exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor → platelets adhere and aggregate, fibrin is deposited → a sterile platelet–fibrin thrombus. This is non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE). NBTE also occurs without any infection in hypercoagulable states — malignancy (marantic endocarditis), SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome (Libman–Sacks), DIC.

NBTE is the substrate. Bacteremia is the seed. IE is the crop.

Step 3 — Transient bacteremia + adherence (the MSCRAMM step). Bacteria enter through mucosal or skin breaches — chewing and toothbrushing, dental work, injection drug use, IV catheters, GI/GU instrumentation. They stick to the NBTE using MSCRAMMs (Microbial Surface Components Recognizing Adhesive Matrix Molecules):

  • S. aureus FnBPA/FnBPB — fibronectin-binding proteins that bridge the bacterium to fibronectin and then to the host α5β1 integrin.
  • S. aureus ClfA (clumping factor A) — binds fibrinogen by a "dock, lock, and latch" mechanism that behaves as a catch-bond: the bond gets stronger under shear. A high-velocity jet does not wash the organism off — it welds it on.
  • Streptococci — FimA and glucans/dextrans synthesized from dietary sucrose. This is the molecular basis of the oral-streptococci–dental link.
  • E. faecalis — Ebp pili, collagen-binding adhesin Ace, aggregation substance.

Step 4 — Vegetation growth and the immunologic sanctuary. Adherent bacteria trigger more platelet activation and tissue-factor expression → more fibrin → the organisms become entombed in a layered platelet–fibrin biofilm. The consequences are the entire reason IE is treated the way it is:

  • Neutrophils, antibody and complement cannot penetrate the fibrin shell — phagocytosis fails. The vegetation is avascular: there is no blood supply to deliver immune cells.
  • Bacterial density reaches 10⁹–10¹¹ CFU/g of vegetation — a burden orders of magnitude beyond an abscess.
  • Deep organisms drop into a metabolically dormant, stationary phase — and β-lactams and glycopeptides only kill actively dividing cells.
This is the through-line of the entire guide. Because the vegetation is avascular, dense, and full of dormant bacteria, IE uniquely demands (1) bactericidal drugs — bacteriostatic agents cannot finish the job when there are no immune cells to help; (2) high doses — to drive drug across an avascular fibrin mass; (3) parenteral or high-bioavailability routes — to hold serum concentrations above the MIC continuously; (4) prolonged courses of 4–6 weeks — to catch each dormant organism in the brief moment it wakes up and divides; and (5) surgery when the sanctuary is simply too big, too destructive, or built on prosthetic material.
The vegetation is a medieval walled castle that the enemy built out of your own bricks. The platelets and fibrin in the wall are your clotting proteins — the bacteria hijacked them. Once the garrison is inside: your infantry can't scale the wall (neutrophils and antibodies never get in); the garrison is asleep (dormant bacteria — and cell-wall antibiotics are weapons that only work on soldiers who are moving); and you cannot win with a short siege (5 days of antibiotics does nothing — you need a continuous, saturating bombardment for 4–6 weeks so that every soldier who wakes up and moves gets killed). And when the walls are simply too thick, you stop besieging and send in the demolition crew — the cardiac surgeon.

Corollary for prosthetic valves: a prosthesis adds a second wall — an abiotic surface with its own biofilm that no antibiotic reliably sterilizes. That is why prosthetic-valve IE gets rifampin (the one drug that penetrates biofilm on foreign material), and why it so often ends in the operating room anyway.
The five-step cascade — and the three places we interrupt it. Prophylaxis blocks step 3 (bacteremia); bactericidal antibiotics attack the mature vegetation; surgery physically removes it.
🌊

Why the vegetation sits where it does — the jet-lesion rule

In 1963 Rodbard modelled cardiac valves as Venturi tubes and aerosolized bacteria through them. Fluid driven from a high-pressure chamber through a narrow orifice creates a low-pressure sink immediately downstream, where flow decelerates, turns turbulent, and deposits particles. The endothelium there gets stripped; the NBTE forms there; the bacteria land there.

The rule: the vegetation grows on the LOW-pressure (downstream) side of the jet. Ask yourself "where is the blood squirting to?" — and that is where you will find the vegetation on the echo.

The jet-lesion rule — the vegetation always grows on the low-pressure (downstream) side of the jet.
LesionHigh-pressure chamberJet flows →Vegetation sits on
Mitral regurgitationLV (~120 mmHg, systole)→ LA (~10 mmHg)Atrial surface of the mitral valve
Aortic regurgitationAorta (~80 mmHg, diastole)→ LV (~10 mmHg, diastole)Ventricular surface of the aortic valve
Aortic stenosisLV→ aortaAortic (downstream) surface
VSDLV→ RVRV side of the defect + the RV free wall where the jet lands ("jet lesion")
PDAAorta→ pulmonary arteryPulmonary-artery side
Why the left side is hit far more than the right. Left-sided pressures — and therefore the pressure gradients across lesions — are roughly five times higher, generating far more shear and endothelial injury. Right-sided IE (<10% of cases) therefore needs either a direct inoculum (injection drug use, indwelling catheters, pacemaker leads) or a high-velocity right-sided jet (VSD). This is also why people who inject drugs get tricuspid disease: the injected bacteria hit the right heart first.

What the lesion actually looks like

Gross pathology — a small granular, red-brown vegetation on the valve line of closure. This is the lesion. Everything else in this guide follows from what it is made of.
Mikael Häggström MD · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
Subacute bacterial endocarditis of the mitral valve (Haemophilus parainfluenzae — a HACEK organism). Note the bulky, friable vegetation destroying the leaflet — the substrate for both acute regurgitation and embolism.
CDC Public Health Image Library (PHIL #851) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Histology (H&E) — acute ulcerative polypoid endocarditis of the aortic valve. The vegetation is a laminated mass of fibrin and platelets with colonies of bacteria buried inside it, and — critically — no blood vessels and almost no neutrophils within the mass. This is the immune sanctuary, visible under the microscope.

💥

The three consequence pathways — every complication is one of these

Once the vegetation exists, it can hurt the patient in exactly three ways. Every complication of IE — and every reason you will be called at 3am — is one of these three.

① LOCAL DESTRUCTION → heart failure, heart block, shunts

Bacterial proteases and host inflammation digest the valve and the tissue around it.

  • Leaflet perforation / chordal rupture → acute severe regurgitation → flash pulmonary edema. The key is that the LA and LV are non-compliant acutely — they have had no time to dilate — so the regurgitant volume translates into a catastrophic pressure rise rather than a tolerated volume load. Heart failure is the most frequent complication of IE and the number-one indication for urgent/emergency surgery (HF occurs in 19–73% of left-sided IE across series; 32% in ICE-PCS).
  • Periannular / perivalvular abscess — the infection burrows out of the valve and into the annulus. Seen in 10–40% of native-valve IE and 56–100% of prosthetic-valve IE; more common with aortic than mitral disease.
  • ★ Aortic root abscess → heart block. The weakest part of the aortic annulus lies right next to the membranous interventricular septum — which contains the AV node and the bundle of His. Infection tracking there interrupts conduction. New AV block has an ~88% positive predictive value for an abscess, but a sensitivity of only ~45% — meaning a new PR prolongation is nearly diagnostic of a root abscess, while a normal ECG does not exclude one. This is why you order a daily ECG and watch the PR interval in aortic-valve IE.
  • Pseudoaneurysm and aorto-cavitary fistula — an abscess cavity pressurized at systemic pressure ruptures into an adjacent chamber. Mortality with aorto-cavitary fistulization is ~41% despite surgery in most.
  • Prosthetic valve dehiscence — annular destruction unseats the sewing ring → paravalvular regurgitation and a rocking prosthesis on echo.
Aortic root abscess on echocardiography (parasternal long axis). A perivalvular echolucent cavity — this is the lesion that produces new AV block, and it is an urgent surgical indication: antibiotics cannot sterilize an abscess.
CardioNetworks / ECHOpedia (AMC Echolab, Amsterdam) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

② EMBOLIC → stroke, splenic/renal infarct, septic PE, mycotic aneurysm

  • Embolic events occur in 20–50% of IE — and roughly half are clinically silent. Stroke occurs in ~17% and non-stroke systemic embolism in ~23% (ICE-PCS). Silent cerebral emboli are found in up to 80% when you go looking with MRI.
  • Left-sided IE embolizes to the brain (most common), then spleen, kidney, liver, mesentery, coronaries, limbs.
  • Right-sided IE embolizes to the lung → septic pulmonary emboli: multiple peripheral, often cavitating nodules. This is the radiographic hallmark of tricuspid IE in people who inject drugs.
  • Mycotic (infective) aneurysm — a septic embolus lodges in the vasa vasorum or the arterial lumen → arteritis → mural destruction → aneurysm → rupture (SAH/ICH). The rupture rate across a systematic review was ~36%. Note the misnomer: "mycotic" means mushroom-shaped, not fungal.
  • Splenic infarcts occur in ~20% and are usually asymptomatic; up to ~5% progress to a splenic abscess, which needs drainage or splenectomy — and which must be dealt with before valve surgery if possible, to avoid seeding the new prosthesis.
  • What drives embolic risk: vegetation size (≥10 mm) and mobility, left-sided location, S. aureus, prior embolism, AF, diabetes, age. Mitral vegetations embolize more than aortic (~25% vs ~10%), and the highest risk of all (~37%) is a vegetation on the anterior mitral leaflet.
  • ★ Embolic risk falls steeply within the first two weeks of effective antibiotics. This is the single most important fact about the timing of surgery-to-prevent-embolism: the benefit is front-loaded. If you are going to operate to prevent a stroke, operating in week 4 is largely closing the barn door.
Splenic infarcts — pale wedge-shaped areas from septic emboli lodging in the splenic arterial tree. Found in ~20% of IE and usually silent; a persistently febrile patient with a splenic lesion needs imaging to exclude progression to splenic abscess.
Narraburra · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

③ IMMUNE-COMPLEX → glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots

Weeks of continuous bacteremia mean weeks of continuous antigen → circulating immune complexes → type III hypersensitivity deposition. These are the findings of subacute disease, because they take weeks to develop.

  • Immune-complex glomerulonephritis — low complement (C3/C4), RBC casts, dysmorphic hematuria, proteinuria, rising creatinine. Distinguish it from a septic embolic renal infarct (flank pain, wedge-shaped defect on CT) and from vancomycin/gentamicin nephrotoxicity (bland sediment, normal complement) — you will be asked to sort out exactly this on rounds.
  • Osler nodes — painful, raised, tender nodules on the finger and toe pulps. Immune-complex vasculitis.
  • Roth spots — retinal hemorrhages with pale/white centers (a fibrin–platelet plug with inflammatory cells).
  • Rheumatoid factor positivity — a marker of prolonged antigenic stimulation, hence a subacute phenomenon. It is a minor Duke criterion.
  • Splenomegaly — reticuloendothelial hyperplasia from chronic antigenemia.
Janeway lesions are NOT immunologic — they are embolic. They are painless erythematous macules on the palms and soles, caused by septic microemboli with microabscesses. The Duke criteria correctly file Janeway lesions under vascular phenomena, and Osler nodes and Roth spots under immunologic phenomena — and exam questions live precisely on that distinction.

"Janeway is painless, on the palm, and embolic. Osler is Ouch, on the pulp, and immune."

By site and material

TypeDefinitionShare of cases & why it matters
Native valve (NVE)No prosthetic material~57–72% (EURO-ENDO 56.6%; ICE-PCS 72%)
Prosthetic valve (PVE)Surgical or transcatheter valve, annuloplasty ring, conduit~21–30%. Higher mortality; needs rifampin; usually needs surgery.
— Early PVE<12 months from implantation (ESC 2023, for choosing empiric antibiotics)Acquired perioperatively → CoNS, S. aureus, Corynebacterium, Candida, Gram-negatives

A source conflict worth knowingESC 2023 uses <12 months to define "early" PVE when selecting empiric antibiotics, but uses <6 months in one of its surgical recommendations. Both cutoffs appear in the same document, for different purposes. If someone corrects your number, this is why.

By tempo — and why the classic picture has mostly disappeared

TempoCourseClassic organismsValve
AcuteDays to ≤2 weeks; high fever, rapid valve destruction, sepsisS. aureus, β-hemolytic strep, S. pneumoniaeOften a structurally normal valve
SubacuteWeeks to months; low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, immune phenomenaViridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, enterococci, HACEKUsually an abnormal/damaged valve
The textbook subacute patient with Osler nodes and Roth spots is now a rarity. In ICE-PCS, 77% of patients presented within 30 days of symptom onset, "with few of the classic clinical hallmarks of IE." Contemporary endocarditis is acute and staphylococcal. If you wait for peripheral stigmata to make the diagnosis, you will miss it — and the patient will embolize while you wait.

By acquisition

  • Community-acquired — ~71%.
  • Healthcare-associated — ~23% (nosocomial ~14% + non-nosocomial healthcare-associated ~9%: dialysis, home infusion, nursing home, recent hospitalization). Think S. aureus, including MRSA.
  • Injection-drug-use associated — ~10% in ICE-PCS and rising sharply with the opioid epidemic; US IE mortality is climbing, especially in young adults.
🦠

Microbiology — who causes it, and in whom

The single most important epidemiologic shift of the last 30 years: Staphylococcus aureus has overtaken viridans streptococci as the leading cause of IE. In ICE-PCS (n = 2,781 across 25 countries), S. aureus caused 31% of cases. In the US it rose from 37.6% (1998) to 49.3% (2009) of pathogen-identified IE. The disease you were taught (indolent, dental, viridans) is not the disease you will admit (acute, staphylococcal, often healthcare- or drug-use-associated).

Organism (ICE-PCS)ShareWhat it tells you
Staphylococcus aureus31%#1. Acute, destructive, normal valves, high embolic risk. S. aureus bacteremia = get an echo, every time.
Viridans group streptococci17%Subacute; oral source; abnormal valves; usually penicillin-susceptible.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci11%Prosthetic material and lines. A single positive set is usually a contaminant — unless there is prosthetic material.
Enterococci10%Elderly, GU/GI instrumentation. Rising. Intrinsically tolerant to β-lactams → needs synergy.
S. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis)6%→ Colonoscopy is mandatory. See the pearl below.
HACEK2%Fastidious Gram-negatives; large vegetations; ceftriaxone-responsive.
Fungi (usually Candida)2%Prosthetic valves, PWID, TPN, immunosuppressed. Mortality >50% — almost always needs surgery.
Culture-negative10%10% in ICE-PCS but 21% in EURO-ENDO, and up to 30% in some series. Worse outcomes.

Match the organism to the setting — this is how you choose empiric therapy

SettingExpectWhy
Native valve, communityS. aureus; viridans strep; enterococci; S. gallolyticusOral, skin and gut flora seeding via transient bacteremia

Culture-negativeCoxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma whipplei, Legionella, fungiIntracellular or fastidious — they will not grow on standard media. You must ask the lab for them specifically.
Streptococcus gallolyticus IE means "find the colon cancer." Between 25% and 80% of patients with S. bovis/gallolyticus bacteremia harbor a colorectal tumor. In one classic series of group-D streptococcal endocarditis, the S. bovis group had colonic polyps in 67% and colonic carcinoma in 18%, versus 21% and 2% in the enterococcal group — the strongest association being with villous/tubulovillous adenomas. Colonoscopy is mandatory, and ESC 2023 explicitly notes that a whole-body CT does not substitute for it. (There is a growing but weaker literature linking E. faecalis IE to occult colorectal neoplasia — reasonable to consider, but not yet a formal guideline recommendation.)
Culture-negative endocarditis. Warthin–Starry silver stain of a cardiac valve showing Bartonella henselae bacilli — an organism that will never grow in a routine blood-culture bottle. Culture-negative IE is 10–21% of cases, and the #1 cause is antibiotics given before the cultures were drawn.
CDC / Warthin–Starry stain · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

Tie every drug to the mechanism it interrupts

This is the map you should carry into every antibiotic decision in this guide. Each drug class attacks one structure in the bacterium — and the peculiarities of the vegetation (avascular, dense, dormant bacteria, sometimes built on plastic) explain every dosing rule that follows.

Where each endocarditis drug hits the bug — and why the vegetation forces high-dose, bactericidal, prolonged therapy.
Drug classMolecular targetWhat it means at the bedside
β-lactams
Pen G, ampicillin, nafcillin, oxacillin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone		Bind penicillin-binding proteins (the transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan) → the wall fails → autolysis. Only kills dividing cells.Time-dependent killing → the goal is to keep free drug above the MIC as close to 100% of the time as possible. That is why the doses look absurd (nafcillin 12 g/day; penicillin G 12–24 million units/day) and why they are given q4h or by continuous infusion — not q12h. And because deep bacteria only divide occasionally, you must hold that level for weeks.
VancomycinBinds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan precursor — it caps the substrate, not the enzyme (which is why β-lactamase cannot touch it).A big molecule → poor vegetation/biofilm penetration and slow bactericidal activity → it is inferior to β-lactams for MSSA and is a fallback, not a co-equal. Efficacy is AUC-driven: target AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600.
DaptomycinCalcium-dependent insertion of its lipid tail into the membrane → oligomerizes → K⁺ efflux → rapid depolarization → death. Kills non-dividing organisms too.Killing dormant bacteria is a genuine advantage inside a vegetation. But: daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — the surfactant sequesters its lipid tail (MIC rises >100-fold with as little as 10% surfactant). Never use daptomycin to treat pneumonia. Monitor CK weekly; it can also cause eosinophilic pneumonia.
Gentamicin
("synergy" dosing)		Binds the 30S ribosome → mistranslation. But it cannot cross the Gram-positive cell wall on its own.A cell-wall-active drug punches the hole that lets the aminoglycoside in — that is true synergy, and it is the whole reason enterococci (intrinsically tolerant to β-lactams — inhibited but not killed) classically needed it. High-level aminoglycoside resistance (HLAR) abolishes the synergy entirely → you must switch to ampicillin + ceftriaxone. Note the synergy dose is 3 mg/kg/day — not the 5–7 mg/kg Gram-negative dose.
RifampinBinds the β-subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase (rpoB) → blocks transcription. Uniquely penetrates biofilm and kills adherent, slow-growing staphylococci on foreign material.① Never monotherapy — the rpoB mutation rate is ~10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸, so resistance emerges in days. ② Prosthetic material only — ESC 2023: "Rifampin should be used only in foreign body infections such as PVE." ③ Start it only AFTER the bacteremia has cleared (see the wards section — this is a genuinely dangerous detail). ④ A potent CYP3A4 inducer — it wrecks warfarin, DOACs, azoles, antiretrovirals, tacrolimus and methadone (→ withdrawal).
Ampicillin + ceftriaxone
(dual β-lactam, for E. faecalis)		E. faecalis has low-affinity PBP4/PBP5. Ampicillin saturates PBP4/5; ceftriaxone saturates PBP2/PBP3. Together → complete PBP saturation → synergistic bactericidal killing.This elegant piece of pharmacology replaces the aminoglycoside entirely — no nephrotoxicity, no ototoxicity, and it works even with HLAR. It is the reason amp+ceftriaxone has displaced amp+gentamicin as the default for E. faecalis IE.
LinezolidBinds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit → blocks the 70S initiation complex. Bacteriostatic against staph/enterococci.A bacteriostatic drug is a poor fit for a bactericidal disease — reserve for VRE or salvage. Watch myelosuppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy beyond 2 weeks, and serotonin syndrome (it is a weak MAO inhibitor).
DoxycyclineBinds 30S → blocks aminoacyl-tRNA docking. The one class with reliable intracellular activity.The backbone of fastidious/culture-negative regimens — Coxiella, Bartonella, T. whipplei, Brucella.
Hydroxychloroquine
(added in Q fever)		Alkalinizes the acidic phagolysosome where Coxiella burnetii lives.Doxycycline is inactive at low pH. Raising the pH converts doxycycline from bacteriostatic to bactericidal against intracellular Coxiella. That is why the regimen is doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine and not doxycycline alone. Requires baseline and 6-monthly eye exams (retinopathy).
Echinocandins / amphotericin BEchinocandins block β-1,3-D-glucan synthase (fungal wall); amphotericin binds ergosterol → membrane pores.Fungal vegetations are bulky and antifungals penetrate them poorly. Fungal IE almost always requires surgery plus long-term azole suppression, and mortality still exceeds 50%.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency, and the mechanism behind each

Every finding in IE comes from one of the three consequence pathways: bacteremia (fever, constitutional symptoms), valve destruction (murmur, heart failure, heart block), embolism (stroke, splenic/renal infarct, Janeway lesions, septic PE), or immune complexes (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor). Read each sign as a clue to which pathway is active.

Frequencies below are from ICE-PCS (Murdoch, Arch Intern Med 2009; n ≈ 2,781 definite IE across 25 countries) unless noted — the largest contemporary prospective cohort.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Fever (>38 °C)96%Continuous bacteremia → IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α → hypothalamic prostaglandin release. The most sensitive finding by far. Its absence should make you doubt the diagnosis — though it can be masked by antipyretics, steroids, age, or renal failure.
Anemia (normocytic)~85%Anemia of inflammation: IL-6 → hepcidin → iron sequestered in macrophages → iron-restricted erythropoiesis, plus marrow suppression and shortened RBC survival. A slowly falling hemoglobin in a febrile patient is a quiet clue.
Elevated CRP62%Acute-phase response. Non-specific, but the best of the inflammatory markers for tracking response (CRP outperformed procalcitonin for IE diagnosis: AUC 0.80 vs 0.71).
Elevated ESR61%Fibrinogen and immunoglobulin-driven rouleaux formation. Slower to move than CRP in both directions.
Any cardiac murmur~65%EURO-ENDO figure. Turbulent flow across a damaged or vegetation-laden valve.
NEW murmur48%New regurgitation from leaflet destruction or chordal rupture. A new murmur is far more meaningful than any murmur — and note the Duke criteria explicitly do not count a worsening pre-existing murmur.
Heart failure32%Acute severe regurgitation into a non-compliant chamber → pressure, not volume, rises → flash pulmonary edema. The most frequent complication and the #1 indication for surgery.
Hematuria26%Two very different causes you must separate: immune-complex GN (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria, low complement) vs septic renal infarct (flank pain, wedge defect on CT, bland sediment).
Systemic embolization (non-stroke)23%Friable vegetation fragments shower the spleen, kidneys, liver, mesentery, coronaries and limbs. About half of all embolic events are clinically silent.
Worsening of a pre-existing murmur20%Progressive damage to an already abnormal valve. Real, but not a Duke criterion — only a genuinely new regurgitant murmur counts.
Stroke17%Left-sided vegetation embolizes to the brain — most often the MCA territory. Risk tracks with vegetation size (≥10 mm), mobility, mitral location and S. aureus. Silent lesions are found on MRI in 60–80%.
Intracardiac abscess14%Infection burrows through the annulus. Aortic ≫ mitral. Watch the PR interval: a new AV block has an 88% PPV for abscess — though only 45% sensitivity, so a normal ECG never excludes one (AHA 2015).
Myalgia / back pain12–15%Immune-complex/vasculitic, and sometimes true spondylodiscitis from hematogenous seeding — which is itself a reason to get a TEE. New back pain in a bacteremic patient is not "just muscular."
Splenomegaly11%Reticuloendothelial hyperplasia from chronic antigenemia — a subacute sign.
Arthralgia10%Immune-complex deposition in synovium; the fluid is characteristically sterile and it resolves rapidly with antibiotics.
Splinter hemorrhages8%Microemboli/vasculitis in the nail-bed capillaries. Notoriously non-specific — also seen in trauma, psoriasis and vasculitis, which is why the number in a "referred for suspected IE" population runs far higher than in confirmed IE.
Janeway lesions5%PAINLESS macules on palms and soles. Septic microemboli with microabscesses → a vascular phenomenon (Duke files it under vascular, not immunologic).
Conjunctival hemorrhage5%Microembolic/vasculitic capillary rupture. A vascular minor criterion.
Positive rheumatoid factor5%Prolonged antigenemia → polyclonal B-cell activation → anti-IgG autoantibody. A marker of duration, hence a subacute finding — and now rare precisely because we diagnose faster.
Osler nodes3%PAINFUL tender nodules on the finger/toe pulps. Immune-complex vasculitis → an immunologic phenomenon.
Roth spots2%Retinal hemorrhage with a pale/white center (a fibrin–platelet plug with inflammatory cells). Immunologic phenomenon.
Stop waiting for the classic stigmata — they are gone. Osler nodes (3%), Janeway lesions (5%), Roth spots (2%) and splenomegaly (11%) are now uncommon, because they take weeks of untreated bacteremia to develop and 77% of contemporary patients present within 30 days of symptom onset. The disease has shifted from indolent viridans-strep-on-a-damaged-valve to acute S. aureus on a normal valve. If you hold out for peripheral stigmata before you believe the diagnosis, the patient will embolize while you wait. Fever + a new murmur, or fever + a positive blood culture, is the modern presentation.
Osler nodes — painful, raised, tender nodules on the finger pulps. Immune-complex vasculitis → an immunologic phenomenon. Present in only ~3% today.
Roberto J. Galindo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Janeway lesion — painless erythematous macule on the palm. Septic microemboli with microabscesses → a vascular phenomenon. ~5%.
Warfieldian · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Splinter hemorrhage — linear subungual microembolic/vasculitic bleed. ~8%, and highly non-specific (trauma, psoriasis, vasculitis).
Splarka · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
The one-line discriminator"Janeway is painless, on the palm, and embolic. Osler is Ouch, on the pulp, and immune." Exam questions live on this distinction, and so does your understanding of the two different mechanisms at work.

TEE for abscessSens 76–100%
Spec 95%		TTE is poor for perivalvular abscess (sensitivity only 18–63%). TEE is the test. (AHA 2015)
Repeat echo5–7 daysClass I. If the first study is negative/inconclusive and suspicion stays high, repeat TTE and/or TEE within 5–7 days — vegetations grow, and an early echo can simply be too early.
Cardiac CTMajor criterionBetter than TEE for perivalvular complications — abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula. Echo remains better for small (<10 mm) vegetations and leaflet perforation. Also gives you the pre-op coronary anatomy.
[18F]FDG PET/CTPVE: sens 86% / spec 84%
Native: sens 36% / spec 99%		Best for prosthetic valves and devices. Nearly useless to rule out native-valve IE (sens 36%) but a positive scan is close to definitive (spec 99%). Requires a 12-h high-fat / low-carbohydrate diet then a 12-h fast — this starves the myocardium onto fatty acids so it stops taking up glucose and stops drowning out the signal. Skipping the prep ruins the scan.
Brain MRILesions in 60–80%Silent cerebral emboli are the norm, not the exception. Symptomatic cerebrovascular events occur in ~35%; MRI finds lesions in 60–80%. Findings change surgical timing decisions (hemorrhage in particular), which is their main value.
CT chestRight-sided IESeptic pulmonary emboli — multiple peripheral/subpleural nodules, often cavitating, sometimes with a feeding vessel. The hallmark of tricuspid IE. Can progress to empyema.
The "3-month PET window." FDG-PET/CT is unreliable within 3 months of valve surgery, because the surgery itself causes inflammatory uptake — BioGlue surgical adhesive and the Medtronic Mosaic bioprosthesis are notorious for it, and false positives have been reported up to a year out. That is exactly why Duke-ISCVID makes PET a major criterion only ≥3 months post-implant, and a minor one before that. ESC 2023 disagrees and drops the window entirely — a genuine disagreement between the two 2023 documents.
Vegetation on the tricuspid valve (arrow) on echocardiography — the lesion the Duke imaging criterion is looking for. Right-sided disease like this is the signature of injection drug use, indwelling catheters and pacemaker leads.
Koya D, Shibuya K, Kikkawa R, Haneda M · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means, why it moves, and what fools it
Blood culturesThe diagnosis. Bacteremia in IE is continuous, so you need not wait for a fever spike. 3 sets, separate venipunctures, 10 mL per bottle, before antibiotics. Falsely negative: prior antibiotics (the #1 cause of culture-negative IE), under-filled bottles, fastidious organisms (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, T. whipplei) that need serology/PCR you must specifically request. Falsely "positive": a single bottle of coagulase-negative staph is usually a contaminant — unless there is prosthetic material, when it becomes a typical organism.
CRP / ESRElevated in ~62% / ~61%. Neither is diagnostic — ESC is explicit that no biomarker has adequate specificity for IE. Their value is trending the response, and as relapse surveillance after therapy ends. A CRP that plateaus or re-rises on appropriate antibiotics means uncontrolled infection — go looking for an abscess, a metastatic focus, or an infected line.
ProcalcitoninDo not rely on it here. Pooled sensitivity 64%, specificity 73% for IE — no threshold gives you both. CRP actually outperforms it (AUC 0.80 vs 0.71). A normal procalcitonin does not exclude endocarditis.
CreatinineAcute renal failure complicates 40–69% of IE; 6% need dialysis, and that subgroup carries ~40% mortality. ESC names five distinct causes, and your job is to say which: ① immune-complex/vasculitic GN · ② septic embolic renal infarct · ③ cardiorenal (hemodynamic) from heart failure · ④ drug toxicity — aminoglycosides, vancomycin, nafcillin/oxacillin, NSAIDs, high-dose loop diuretics · ⑤ contrast nephropathy. They have different treatments, so name the mechanism before you act.
UrinalysisHematuria in ~26%. Dysmorphic RBCs + RBC casts + proteinuria → immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Isolated hematuria + flank pain, bland sediment → renal infarct from a septic embolus. Sterile pyuria + WBC casts + eosinophilia + rash → think nafcillin-induced acute interstitial nephritis, not the endocarditis at all.
Complement C3/C4Low C3 and C4 together = classical-pathway consumption by immune complexes — supports IE-associated GN. Caveat worth knowing: some IE-associated GN runs through the alternative pathway with normal complement, so a normal C3/C4 does not exclude it.
Rheumatoid factorPositive in only ~5% today — a marker of prolonged antigenic stimulation, so it belongs to the subacute picture. It is a minor Duke criterion when positive.
Troponin / NT-proBNPBoth are associated with worse prognosis in IE. Troponin rises from myocardial strain, demand ischemia, or (rarely) septic coronary embolism; natriuretic peptides rise with the acute volume/pressure load of a destroyed valve. No validated IE-specific cutoff exists — use them as prognostic texture, not decision thresholds.
LactateThe operational marker of shock. Septic shock = vasopressors needed to hold MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume (Sepsis-3, adopted by ESC). It happens in 5–10% of IE — and it is an ICU trigger.
WBCLeukocytosis is typical of acute IE; the subacute patient is more often anemic with a near-normal count. ESC explicitly declines to give it diagnostic weight — a normal white count does not exclude endocarditis.
Shared

Diagnosis — cultures, echo, Duke

🩸

Blood cultures — the one thing you must not get wrong

Blood cultures are the single highest-yield test in IE, and the single most commonly botched one. The bacteremia of IE is continuous (the vegetation sheds organisms into the bloodstream constantly) — which is why you do not need to wait for a fever spike, and why a well-collected set is positive in the great majority of untreated cases.

3 setsThree separate sets from separate venipunctures. A "set" = one aerobic + one anaerobic bottle drawn at the same time.Always
10 mL per bottleVolume is the strongest determinant of yield — under-filling the bottle is the most common reason a true bacteremia is missed. Fill them properly.Always
BEFORE antibioticsThe number-one cause of culture-negative IE is antibiotics given before the cultures were drawn. If the patient is stable, draw first. If they are septic, draw and give antibiotics immediately — do not delay antibiotics in sepsis to chase cultures.Critical
Tell the labIf you suspect a fastidious organism, say "possible endocarditis" — ask for prolonged incubation and add serology/PCR for Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, T. whipplei. They will not look for these unless you ask.If culture-negative
What changed in 2023The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria removed the old requirements for specific timing (draws >12 h apart; 3/3 or a majority of ≥4 drawn ≥1 h apart) and for separate venipuncture sites from the criteria themselves. What now matters is simply the number of positive sets: ≥2 sets for a typical organism, ≥3 sets for a non-typical one. Separate venipunctures remain strongly recommended as good microbiologic practice — they just are no longer part of the criteria. Note that ESC 2023 kept the old timing rules in its own criteria; this is a real divergence between the two 2023 documents.
Staphylococcus aureus in the blood is never a contaminant. A single positive set of S. aureus demands a search for endocarditis — echocardiography, every time. Conversely, a single set growing coagulase-negative staph is usually a contaminant — unless there is prosthetic material in the heart, in which case CoNS becomes a typical organism and the same set becomes meaningful. Context changes the meaning of the identical lab result.
🧭

The diagnostic pathway

Diagnostic pathway — cultures first, then TTE, then TEE, then advanced imaging, then apply the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria.
🧮

2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria — interactive

Fowler, CID 2023

Check what your patient has. Majors are counted by category — microbiologic, imaging and surgical each contribute at most one major, however many sub-items are satisfied (this mirrors the original Duke structure, where "positive blood cultures" and "endocardial involvement" were each a single major criterion).

Pathologic criteria — either alone = DEFINITE
Organisms identified (culture, stain, PCR/sequencing, ISH) in a vegetation, cardiac tissue, explanted valve/sewing ring, CIED, or an arterial embolus
Active endocarditis identified histologically in/on a vegetation or the above tissue
Major — Microbiologic (any one → 1 major)
Typical organism from ≥2 separate blood-culture sets
Non-typical organism from ≥3 separate blood-culture sets
Positive blood PCR / nucleic-acid test for C. burnetii, Bartonella spp., or T. whipplei
C. burnetii anti-phase I IgG >1:800, or isolated from a single blood culture
Bartonella henselae/quintana IFA IgG ≥1:800
Major — Imaging (any one → 1 major)
Echo or cardiac CT: vegetation, leaflet perforation, leaflet aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, or intracardiac fistula
New significant valvular regurgitation, or new partial prosthetic dehiscence (vs prior imaging)
[18F]FDG PET/CT uptake on valve / aortic graft / CIED leads / prosthetic material — ≥3 months after implantation
Major — Surgical (new in 2023)
IE documented by direct inspection during cardiac surgery
Minor criteria (each → 1 minor)
Predisposition — prior IE, prosthetic valve (surgical or transcatheter), prior valve repair, congenital heart disease, more than mild regurgitation or stenosis of any cause, CIED, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, or injection drug use
Fever — documented temperature >38.0 °C (100.4 °F)
Vascular phenomena — arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, cerebral or splenic abscess, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, purulent purpura
Immunologic phenomena — rheumatoid factor, Osler nodes, Roth spots, immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Microbiologic evidence falling short of a major criterion (incl. positive culture/PCR from a sterile site other than cardiac tissue)
Imaging — abnormal PET/CT uptake within 3 months of prosthetic implantation
Physical exam — new valvular regurgitation on auscultation, only if echo is unavailable (a changing pre-existing murmur does not count)
REJECTED
0 major · 0 minor
The thresholds — memorize these DEFINITE = pathologic criteria  ·  OR 2 major  ·  OR 1 major + 3 minor  ·  OR 5 minor
POSSIBLE = 1 major + 1 minor  ·  OR 3 minor
REJECTED = firm alternate diagnosis  ·  OR resolution with <4 days of antibiotics  ·  OR no pathologic evidence at surgery/autopsy after <4 days of antibiotics  ·  OR simply does not reach "Possible".
Shorthand: DEFINITE = 2 / 1+3 / 5.   POSSIBLE = 1+1 / 3.
"Possible IE" is not "probably not IE." It means the criteria have not yet been met — and the criteria were built for research classification, not to tell you whether to treat. Never withhold treatment from a patient you clinically believe has endocarditis just because they score "Possible." Repeat the echo in 5–7 days, chase advanced imaging, and treat.

Which "typical" organism list?

Always typical (≥2 sets)Typical ONLY if prosthetic/intracardiac material is present
Staphylococcus aureus · S. lugdunensis (new) · Enterococcus faecalis (new — and typical regardless of source) · all streptococci except S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes (expanded) · Granulicatella, Abiotrophia, Gemella (new) · HACEK group Coagulase-negative staphylococci · Corynebacterium striatum, C. jeikeium · Serratia marcescens · Pseudomonas aeruginosa · Cutibacterium acnes · non-tuberculous mycobacteria (esp. M. chimaera — the heater–cooler unit outbreaks) · Candida spp.
Why adding E. faecalis mattered so muchMaking E. faecalis a typical organism regardless of the source was the single biggest sensitivity gain in the 2023 revision — it raised sensitivity for definite IE from 70% to 96% in the validating cohort without costing specificity. Non-faecalis enterococci were deliberately not included: they cause IE too rarely. Overall, 2023 Duke-ISCVID sensitivity is ~84% vs ~75% for Modified Duke 2000, at essentially unchanged specificity (~94%).
ESC 2023 publishes its OWN criteria, and they are not identical to Duke-ISCVID. Both came out in 2023 and they genuinely disagree in places:
  • PET/CT timing: Duke-ISCVID makes PET/CT a major criterion only ≥3 months after prosthetic implantation (and minor before that). ESC dropped the 3-month window entirely — for ESC it is major irrespective of the interval from surgery, reasoning that an intense focal/heterogeneous uptake pattern can be told apart from post-op inflammation.
  • Blood-culture timing: Duke-ISCVID removed the timing/venipuncture rules. ESC kept them (≥2 cultures drawn >12 h apart, etc.).
  • Modality: ESC also accepts WBC-SPECT/CT as a major imaging criterion; Duke-ISCVID does not list it.
  • Surgical major criterion: Duke-ISCVID only. ESC has none.
  • Typical-organism list: ESC's is much shorter (oral streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, S. aureus, E. faecalis).
The Definite thresholds (2 / 1+3 / 5) are the same in both. For US boards, use Duke-ISCVID; at the bedside, know that your cardiologist may be applying ESC's version — and that head-to-head, Duke-ISCVID tends to be more sensitive while ESC is more specific.
🩺 Clinic — suspicion, prevention & the outpatient positive blood culture
Assess

When to suspect it

🔍

How IE walks into a clinic

IE is rarely diagnosed in clinic — but it is very often missed there. The outpatient encounter is where the subacute patient gets labelled "viral syndrome" and sent home with a course of oral antibiotics that sterilizes their blood cultures for weeks. Your job in clinic is suspicion and referral, not treatment.

The five ways it shows up

Fever + murmurThe classic. Any new regurgitant murmur in a febrile patient is endocarditis until proven otherwise. A worsening old murmur is softer evidence — and is not a Duke criterion.Classic
Subacute FUOWeeks of low-grade fever, night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, unintentional weight loss — often with a normocytic anemia and a raised ESR/CRP. This is viridans strep or enterococcus on a damaged valve.Subacute
A positive blood cultureS. aureus bacteremia is an emergency — see below. So is enterococcal or viridans-strep bacteremia without an obvious source.Emergency
Embolic event, no sourceStroke in a young person, splenic or renal infarct, an "embolic stroke of undetermined source," or a mycotic aneurysm. Ask where the clot came from — sometimes the answer is a valve.Embolic
The high-risk host with a feverProsthetic valve, prior IE, congenital heart disease, an intracardiac device, hemodialysis, or injection drug use. In these patients the pre-test probability is so high that fever alone justifies cultures and an echo.High risk
Staphylococcus aureus in an outpatient blood culture is a same-day admission. Not a phone call, not oral antibiotics, not "let's recheck next week." S. aureus bacteremia requires inpatient IV therapy, source-control evaluation, repeat cultures to document clearance, and echocardiography in essentially every case (ESC Class IIa — and IDSA practice makes it near-universal). It destroys valves in days, embolizes to the brain, and carries the highest mortality of the common IE organisms. The patient who "looks well" is exactly the one who gets sent home and comes back with a stroke.
What NOT to do in clinic. Do not start empiric oral antibiotics in a stable patient you suspect of IE before cultures are drawn — you will convert a diagnosable illness into culture-negative endocarditis, which has worse outcomes and is the single most common own-goal in this disease. Do not accept a single blood-culture set. Do not defer the echo because they look well.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The outpatient workup — and when it stops being outpatient

Blood cultures ×3Before any antibiotic. Three sets, separate venipunctures, 10 mL per bottle. This is the single highest-yield thing you will do.First
CBC, CMP, CRP/ESRNormocytic anemia, raised inflammatory markers, and a baseline creatinine before anyone gives vancomycin or gentamicin.First
UrinalysisLooking for hematuria/RBC casts (immune-complex GN) — a minor criterion and a clue to chronicity.First
ECGBaseline PR interval. You need the baseline to detect the new AV block that signals a root abscess later.First
TTEIn every suspected case, as soon as possible — earlier echo means fewer embolic events. But remember TTE misses ~30% of native and ~50% of prosthetic IE: a negative TTE does not send the patient home.Urgent
Serology / PCRIf cultures stay negative: Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma whipplei. The lab will not look unless you ask.If culture-neg
ColonoscopyMandatory if S. gallolyticus (S. bovis) — ~65% have a colonic adenoma or carcinoma. A whole-body CT does not substitute for it.Organism-driven
Anything that raises real suspicion of IE gets admitted. There is no outpatient pathway for the diagnostic workup of endocarditis: it needs serial cultures, time-sensitive TEE, IV therapy, and monitoring for complications that evolve over hours.
Prevent

Antibiotic prophylaxis — the tool

🛡️

Does this patient need prophylaxis before their dental work?

AHA 2021 · ESC 2023

This is the endocarditis question you will actually be asked in clinic — usually by a dentist, on the phone. The rule is simple and widely got wrong: you need BOTH a highest-risk cardiac condition AND a qualifying dental procedure. Neither alone is enough.

1 · Cardiac condition
Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material — surgical or transcatheter valve; annuloplasty ring or clip; LVAD or total artificial heart
Previous infective endocarditis (including relapse/recurrence)
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, incl. palliative shunts and conduits
Repaired CHD with prosthetic material — during the first 6 months after the procedure
Repaired CHD with a residual defect at or adjacent to a prosthetic patch/device
Cardiac transplant recipient who develops valvulopathy
None of the above — e.g. pacemaker/ICD, bicuspid aortic valve, MVP, rheumatic heart disease, HCM, coronary stent, dialysis graft
3 · Penicillin allergy?
No allergy — and can take oral
No allergy — but cannot take oral
Penicillin allergy — non-anaphylactic (e.g. rash)
Penicillin allergy — anaphylaxis, angioedema, or urticaria
2 · Procedure
Dental procedure manipulating gingival tissue or the periapical region of the teeth, or perforating the oral mucosa — extraction, periodontal or implant surgery, oral biopsy, scaling, root canal
Not a qualifying procedure — dental x-rays, anesthetic injection through non-infected tissue, removable prosthodontic/orthodontic appliances, orthodontic brackets, shedding of primary teeth, lip/oral-mucosa trauma
A non-dental procedure — GI/GU endoscopy, bronchoscopy, TEE, cystoscopy, childbirth
—
Choose a cardiac condition and a procedure.
The three things everybody gets wrong. ① Pacemakers and ICDs are NOT on the list. A CIED alone does not earn dental prophylaxis — in either AHA or ESC. (Antibiotics at the time of device implantation are a different, procedure-directed indication.) ② Non-dental procedures do not get prophylaxis. No GI/GU endoscopy, no bronchoscopy, no TEE, no childbirth — AHA's 2023 science advisory found no evidence of a causal link. ③ Clindamycin is dead. Both AHA 2021 and ESC 2023 removed it — not for lack of efficacy, but because of fatal C. difficile infection. Up to 15% of community C. difficile may be attributable to antibiotics prescribed for dental procedures.
SituationDrugAdult doseWhen
StandardAmoxicillin2 g POSingle dose, 30–60 min before
Cannot take oralAmpicillin2 g IM/IVSingle dose, 30–60 min before
Cannot take oral (alt)Cefazolin or ceftriaxone1 g IM/IVSingle dose, 30–60 min before
PCN allergy (non-anaphylactic)Cephalexin2 g POOr another 1st/2nd-gen oral cephalosporin
PCN allergyAzithromycin or clarithromycin500 mg POSafe in anaphylaxis
PCN allergyDoxycycline100 mg POSafe in anaphylaxis
PCN anaphylaxisNOT a cephalosporin—Cephalosporins are contraindicated after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin/ampicillin

Doses are identical in AHA 2021 and ESC 2023. If the dose is forgotten, AHA permits giving it up to 2 hours after the procedure.

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & whole-patient prevention

✅

Grade A & B screening for the endocarditis-risk population

The population that gets endocarditis today — especially people who inject drugs — is a population with a specific, high-yield preventive-care bundle that is routinely missed while everyone focuses on the valve. Rates below are current USPSTF grades.

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AHIV screeningAdolescents & adults 15–65 y (and all pregnant persons); younger/older if at increased risk
ASyphilis screeningAsymptomatic non-pregnant adolescents & adults at increased risk
AHepatitis B screening (pregnant)All pregnant women, at the first prenatal visit
ATobacco cessation — ask, advise, behavioral intervention + FDA-approved pharmacotherapyAll non-pregnant adults
BHepatitis C screeningAdults 18–79 y
BHepatitis B screening (non-pregnant)Adolescents & adults at increased risk
BUnhealthy drug use screeningAdults ≥18 y — when diagnosis, treatment and care can be offered or referred
BUnhealthy alcohol use screening + brief behavioral counselingAdults ≥18 y, in primary care
The most effective endocarditis prevention you can offer a person who injects drugs is not an antibiotic — it is treatment for the opioid use disorder. Buprenorphine or methadone reduces all-cause and overdose mortality by roughly half. Add sterile-equipment access and skin-hygiene counseling, plus HCV/HIV/HBV screening. Antibiotic prophylaxis has no role here at all — injection-related IE is a skin-flora inoculation problem, not a dental one.

Dental care is the real prophylaxis

AHA is explicit that maintaining good oral health and regular dental care is more important for preventing viridans streptococcal IE than antibiotic prophylaxis for an isolated procedure. The cumulative bacteremia from chewing and brushing with diseased gums, every day for a year, vastly exceeds the bacteremia of one dental extraction. Refer your high-risk valve patients to a dentist — that is the intervention with the biggest denominator.

Escalate

Red flags → ED / admission

🚑

Don't manage these in clinic

Send to the ED / admit today for any of:
  • Any positive blood culture with a typical IE organism — especially S. aureus, which is never a contaminant.
  • Fever + a new regurgitant murmur.
  • Fever + prosthetic valve, prior IE, CIED, or injection drug use — the pre-test probability alone justifies admission.
  • Any embolic phenomenon — stroke, TIA, limb ischemia, flank pain with hematuria, a painful blue digit.
  • New heart failure, dyspnea, or orthopnea in someone with a murmur — this is acute valve failure until proven otherwise.
  • Syncope, bradycardia, or a new conduction abnormality — a new AV block means a root abscess until proven otherwise (88% PPV).
  • A definite or possible Duke score on the criteria above.
The honest rule: if you are seriously entertaining endocarditis, the patient is admitted. There is no safe outpatient diagnostic pathway. Draw the cultures, then send them in — and make sure the ED knows the cultures are already drawn, so nobody gives antibiotics before the rest are collected.
🛏️ Wards — antibiotics, daily vigilance & the surgical question
Admit

Who to admit & who to call

📋

Admission criteria — and the Endocarditis Team

Every patient with suspected IE is admitted. There is no outpatient pathway, because the workup itself requires things you can only do inpatient: serial blood cultures to confirm the diagnosis and later document clearance, a time-sensitive TEE, immediate IV bactericidal therapy, and hour-by-hour monitoring for complications — a leaflet can rupture, a root abscess can block the AV node, and a vegetation can embolize to the brain, all overnight.

Call the Endocarditis Team on day one — this is now Class I. ESC 2023 upgraded the multidisciplinary "Endocarditis Team" from Class IIa to Class I, Level B. It is not a formality: team-based care measurably reduces mortality. The team is cardiology + cardiac surgery + infectious diseases + microbiology + imaging, and — for the population you will actually be treating — addiction medicine and an OPAT specialist. Any IE patient sick enough for the ICU must be discussed with the team urgently.
Name the four things that decide this patient's course on day one: ① What is the organism? (drives the drug and the duration) ② Native or prosthetic? (drives rifampin, and the likelihood of surgery) ③ Left or right? (drives whether you fear stroke or septic PE) ④ Is there a surgical indication right now? (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, embolic risk). Everything else follows from those four answers.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

What to order on admission

TelemetryContinuous — for exactly the conduction disease above.Admit

Brain imagingIf any neurologic symptom. MRI > CT. Findings change surgical timing — a hemorrhage is the thing that will delay the operation.If symptoms
ColonoscopyIf S. gallolyticus — mandatory, ~65% harbor colonic neoplasia. Arrange before discharge.Organism-driven
Treat

Antibiotics — empiric → targeted

💊

The ladder: cover broadly, then narrow the moment the organism is named

Remember what you are dosing into: an avascular fibrin biofilm with 10⁹–10¹¹ bacteria per gram, most of them dormant, with no neutrophils to help. That is why every regimen below is bactericidal, parenteral, high-dose and long. There is no "titration" the way there is in heart failure — you start at the full target dose on day one and the only things you titrate are the levels (vancomycin AUC, gentamicin peak/trough) and the renal dose adjustment.
1
Empiric — before the organism is known
Cover staph, strep, enterococcus. Then narrow within 24–48 h.
▾

ESC 2023 gives two empiric regimens, split by whether there is prosthetic material and how it was acquired. The moment the organism and its susceptibilities are back — usually 24–48 h — you must narrow. Empiric therapy is a bridge, not a plan.

SettingRegimen & doseWhy these drugsClass
Community-acquired native valve, or late PVE (≥12 mo post-op) Ampicillin 12 g/day IV in 4–6 doses
+ Ceftriaxone 4 g/day IV in 2 doses or (flu)cloxacillin 12 g/day IV in 4–6 doses
+ Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV in 1 dose		 Ampicillin covers enterococcus and streptococci; cloxacillin (or nafcillin/oxacillin in the US) covers MSSA; gentamicin adds synergy. Late PVE behaves microbiologically like native disease. IIa C
Early PVE (<12 mo post-op), nosocomial, or healthcare-associated Vancomycin 30 mg/kg/day IV in 2 doses or daptomycin 10 mg/kg/day IV in 1 dose
+ Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV in 1 dose
+ Rifampin 900–1200 mg/day IV/PO in 2–3 doses		 Must cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci and CoNS (the perioperative sewing-ring organisms) and ideally non-HACEK Gram-negatives. Rifampin is included because there is foreign material. IIb C
If the patient has already had antibiotics, tell the team. ESC is explicit that prior antibiotic exposure should change your empiric choice — and it is also the reason the cultures may never grow anything.
2
Targeted — streptococci & enterococci
The MIC decides the regimen. Read the micro report.

4 wk if symptoms <3 mo; 6 wk if ≥3 mo or PVE		The classic synergy regimen. Note the divided dosing: AHA gives this a Class I — gentamicin must be given in multiple divided daily doses, not once daily, for enterococcal IE. Target peak 3–4 µg/mL, trough <1 µg/mL.
HLAR
(high-level aminoglycoside resistance)		Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h + Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h6 weeksHLAR (growth at gentamicin ≥500 µg/mL) abolishes the synergy entirely — a wide-open cell wall no longer helps, because the ribosome itself is protected. The aminoglycoside is now pure toxicity with zero benefit. Switch to the double β-lactam. If streptomycin-susceptible, streptomycin 7.5 mg/kg IV/IM q12h is an alternative.
VREDaptomycin 10–12 mg/kg/24 h or linezolid 600 mg IV/PO q12h≥6 weeksNot a guideline-graded dose — get ID involved. Linezolid is bacteriostatic, which is a poor fit for a disease that needs killing. Watch cytopenias.
Enterococcal IE always means: send the HLAR screen, and look at the colon. The HLAR result decides whether gentamicin is a drug or just a kidney injury. And enterococcal bacteremia in an older adult should prompt the same question you ask for S. gallolyticus: where did it come from? (GU/GI instrumentation — and consider the colon.)
3
Targeted — staphylococci (the #1 organism)
MSSA vs MRSA, and native vs prosthetic. Four different answers.
▾
ScenarioExact doseDurationWhy / alternative
MSSA, native valveNafcillin or oxacillin 12 g/24 h IV in 4–6 equally divided doses (i.e. 2 g q4h)6 weeksA β-lactam is decisively better than vancomycin for MSSA — never "just leave them on vanc" once you know it is methicillin-susceptible. The huge, q4h dosing is because killing is time-dependent: you need free drug above the MIC essentially 100% of the time.
MSSA, native — uncomplicated RIGHT-sidedNafcillin/oxacillin, same dose2 weeksA genuine exception in AHA 2015 — but only if truly uncomplicated (no left-sided involvement, no metastatic focus, no renal failure, vegetation not huge). Complicated right-sided disease and all left-sided disease get 6 weeks.
MSSA, native — penicillin allergy (non-anaphylactoid)Cefazolin 6 g/24 h IV in 3 divided doses (2 g q8h)6 weeksBetter tolerated than nafcillin. Caveat — the "cefazolin inoculum effect": some MSSA hyperproduce a β-lactamase that chews up cefazolin at the enormous bacterial densities found inside a vegetation. Favor nafcillin/oxacillin for large vegetations or abscesses. Cephalosporins are contraindicated in anaphylactoid β-lactam allergy → use vancomycin.
MRSA, native valveVancomycin, AUC-guided (see the dosing module below) — AHA writes it as 30 mg/kg/24 h IV in 2 divided doses
or Daptomycin ≥8 mg/kg/dose (ESC: 10 mg/kg once daily)		6 weeksDaptomycin is Class IIb in AHA. Note the guideline dose is well above the 6 mg/kg FDA label. Never use daptomycin for pneumonia — surfactant inactivates it. (It is still fine for the intravascular septic emboli of right-sided IE.)
Staph, PROSTHETIC valve
the 3-drug regimen		Nafcillin/oxacillin 12 g/24 h in 6 divided doses (MSSA) or vancomycin (MRSA)
+ Rifampin 900 mg/24 h IV/PO in 3 divided doses (300 mg q8h)
+ Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/24 h IV/IM in 2–3 divided doses		β-lactam/vanc ≥6 weeks
Rifampin ≥6 weeks
Gentamicin 2 weeks only		Rifampin is the only drug that penetrates biofilm on foreign material and kills the adherent, slow-growing staphylococci living on the sewing ring. That is why it appears here and nowhere else.
Do NOT start rifampin on day one. Add it only after 3–5 days of effective therapy, once the bacteremia has cleared. With a high circulating bacterial burden, rifampin resistance is selected almost immediately (rpoB mutates at ~10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸, so a vegetation with 10¹⁰ organisms already contains resistant mutants). In one series, starting rifampin during active bacteremia produced rifampin resistance in 56%, with longer bacteremia (5.2 vs 2.1 days), lower survival (79% vs 95%), and more hepatitis. And never, ever give rifampin alone.
Know the weak spot in this recommendationThe 3-drug PVE regimen is guideline-standard, but be aware the evidence is thin: ARREST (adjunctive rifampicin in S. aureus bacteremia) was negative, and recent meta-analyses found no clear mortality or relapse benefit from adjunctive rifampin or gentamicin in staphylococcal PVE — with more adverse events and drug interactions. It remains the recommendation; it is not settled science. Say so on rounds and you will sound like you have read the literature, because you will have.
Gentamicin is NOT added for native-valve staph IE any more. Cosgrove (CID 2009) showed that even low-dose adjunctive gentamicin caused significant nephrotoxicity with no benefit in mortality or bacteremia clearance. AHA withdrew the recommendation; ESC agrees ("aminoglycosides are not recommended for staphylococcal NVE"). Adding it is a pure-harm move — and a classic intern error.

Targeted — HACEK, culture-negative & fungal
The organisms that need you to think.
▾

HACEK

DrugDoseDurationNotes
Ceftriaxone (first-line)2 g/24 h IV/IM in 1 dose4 wk native
6 wk prosthetic		Almost all HACEK strains are ceftriaxone-susceptible.
Ampicillin-sulbactam12 g/24 h IV in 4 divided doses4 wk / 6 wkAlternative; in-vitro resistance is described.

Assume HACEK is ampicillin-RESISTANT. β-lactamase–producing strains are increasingly common, and these organisms frequently fail to grow well enough for valid susceptibility testing (in one survey 60% of isolates gave no valid result). AHA therefore makes it Class III — do not use penicillin or ampicillin for HACEK IE unless you have susceptibility data proving you can. Note also that gentamicin is no longer recommended for HACEK (nephrotoxicity without benefit).

Culture-negative IE — the organisms your lab will not find unless you ask

OrganismRegimen & doseDurationThe key mechanism
Coxiella burnetii
(Q fever)		Doxycycline 200 mg/24 h PO
+ Hydroxychloroquine 200–600 mg/24 h PO		≥18 months native
≥24 months prosthetic		Coxiella lives in the acidic phagolysosome, where doxycycline is inactive. Hydroxychloroquine alkalinizes that compartment, converting doxycycline from bacteriostatic to bactericidal. That is why the pair is mandatory — and why doxycycline alone fails. The first thing to do about "culture-negative endocarditis" is to ask whether you made it culture-negative. Prior antibiotics are the number-one cause. The second thing is to phone the lab: none of the organisms above grow in a routine bottle, and nobody will run Coxiella/Bartonella serology or 16S PCR unless you specifically request it.
🎚️

The two drugs you actually titrate — vancomycin & gentamicin

DrugStartAdjust / titrate byTarget & maxMonitor
Vancomycin Loading: 20–35 mg/kg IV (actual body weight), max 3,000 mg
Then 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h		 Calculate the AUC (Bayesian software, or 2 levels in a dosing interval) at 24–48 h. Adjust the dose/interval to hit the AUC — not the trough. AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 (assuming MIC = 1)
Trough-only 15–20 is NO LONGER recommended — it over-doses patients into avoidable AKI.		 Creatinine daily while unstable, weekly when stable. Avoid piperacillin-tazobactam alongside it — the combination raises AKI risk (adjusted OR ~3.2). Watch for infusion reaction (histamine-mediated, not an allergy — slow the rate).
Gentamicin
"synergy" dosing		 3 mg/kg/24 h — not the 5–7 mg/kg Gram-negative dose How you divide it depends on the organism:
• Enterococcus → 2–3 DIVIDED doses (AHA Class I — not once daily)
• Viridans strep 2-wk course → SINGLE daily dose
• Staph PVE → 2–3 divided doses		 Divided (enterococcal): peak 3–4 µg/mL, trough <1 µg/mL
Once-daily (ESC): peak (1 h post) 10–12 mg/L, trough <1 mg/L
Max 240 mg/day (ESC)		 Creatinine + levels — check around the 3rd dose, then at least weekly (more often if renal function is moving). Ask about tinnitus, hearing loss and vertigo at every encounter — ototoxicity can be permanent. Consider audiometry beyond 2 weeks.
Why the gentamicin target is so much lower than you expect. In Gram-negative sepsis you want a high peak, because aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent. In endocarditis you are not asking gentamicin to kill anything — you are asking it to potentiate the cell-wall agent. You want the lowest dose that achieves synergy, because every extra milligram is pure nephro- and ototoxicity. That is the whole logic of "synergy dosing."
Score

VIRSTA — does this bacteremia need a TEE?

🧮

VIRSTA score — echo triage in S. aureus bacteremia

Tubiana, J Infect 2016

S. aureus bacteremia is common; endocarditis complicates a minority of it. VIRSTA is the score ESC 2023 itself cites to decide how urgently a patient needs echocardiography.

Cerebral or peripheral emboli +5
Meningitis +5
Permanent intracardiac device or previous IE +4
Injection drug use +4
Pre-existing native valve disease +3
Persistent bacteremia (48-h culture still positive) +3
Vertebral osteomyelitis +2
Community-acquired / non-nosocomial acquisition +2
Severe sepsis or septic shock +1
CRP >190 mg/L +1
0
Do not use VIRSTA to talk yourself out of an echo. A validation study found it is not reliable enough to exclude IE without echocardiography, and both ESC and IDSA still recommend echo in essentially all S. aureus bacteremia. VIRSTA tells you how fast you need the TEE — not whether you can skip it.

Other validated echo-triage scores, deliberately linked out rather than reimplemented here: PREDICT (day-5 score <2 → TEE can be deferred, in SAB) and DENOVA (≥3 → get an echo, in monomicrobial E. faecalis bacteremia).
