Daily management

📈

What to check every single morning

WhatHow oftenWhat you're looking for — and what it means
ECG — the PR intervalDAILYThe highest-yield 30 seconds of your day. A new AV block = aortic root abscess (88% PPV) = urgent surgery. It is silent until it isn't. This is the single most commonly missed finding on the wards.
Blood culturesq24–48 h until negativeYou must document clearance. Persistently positive cultures mean uncontrolled infection — and >1 week of positive cultures on appropriate antibiotics is a Class IIa indication for urgent surgery. It also gates rifampin (start only after clearance).
New murmur / examDailyA new regurgitant murmur means the valve is being destroyed now. Also examine for new emboli — fingers, conjunctivae, abdomen, neuro.
Temperature curveDailyShould defervesce on effective therapy. Persistent fever → go looking: perivalvular abscess, metastatic focus (splenic/psoas/vertebral), an infected line, or drug fever (a common and under-diagnosed cause, especially with β-lactams).
CreatinineDaily on vanc/gentAKI complicates 40–69% of IE. When it rises, name the mechanism: immune-complex GN · septic renal infarct · cardiorenal · drug toxicity · contrast. They are not treated the same.
CRPEvery 2–3 daysA trend, not a number. Falling = responding. Plateau or re-rise = uncontrolled infection — image again.
Drug levelsPer drugVancomycin AUC at 24–48 h then per stability; gentamicin peak/trough around the 3rd dose then weekly. LFTs if on rifampin. CK weekly on daptomycin.
The 3 surgical questionsDAILYHeart failure? Uncontrolled infection? High embolic risk? The answer can change overnight. See below.
Surgery

The three surgical questions

🔪

Roughly half of all IE patients end up having surgery — ask every day

ESC 2023

Surgery is not a failure of medical therapy — for many patients it is the therapy. Antibiotics cannot sterilize an abscess, cannot un-destroy a valve, and cannot reliably clear a biofilm on a prosthesis. ESC defines the timing precisely: emergency = within 24 hours · urgent = within 3–5 days · non-urgent = during the same admission.

The three surgical questions. Ask them EVERY day: heart failure? uncontrolled infection? high embolic risk? The answer can change overnight.
IndicationTimingClass
① HEART FAILURE — the most frequent indication
Severe acute regurgitation, obstruction, or fistula causing refractory pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shockEMERGENCY — within 24 hI B
Severe acute regurgitation or obstruction with HF symptoms, or echo signs of poor hemodynamic toleranceURGENT — within 3–5 dI B
② UNCONTROLLED INFECTION
Abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, prosthetic dehiscence, new AV blockURGENT — 3–5 dI B
Fungal or multi-resistant organismUrgent / non-urgentI C
Blood cultures still positive >1 week despite appropriate antibiotics (or persistent sepsis) with metastatic foci controlledUrgent — should be consideredIIa B
PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negativesUrgent — should be consideredIIa C
③ PREVENTION OF EMBOLISM — note it's ≥10 mm, not >10 mm
Persistent vegetation ≥10 mm after ≥1 embolic episode despite appropriate antibioticsURGENTI B
Vegetation ≥10 mm + another indication for surgeryURGENTI C
Vegetation ≥10 mm, no severe valve dysfunction, no embolism, and low surgical riskUrgent — may be consideredIIb B
RIGHT-sided: residual tricuspid vegetation >20 mm after recurrent septic pulmonary emboliSurgery recommendedI C
Two numbers people get wrong. ① The left-sided embolic threshold is ≥10 mm (greater-than-or-equal-to). ② The often-quoted ">15 mm" and ">30 mm" figures are not ESC 2023 recommendation thresholds — ">15 mm" was the 2015 guideline (now superseded) and ">30 mm" appears only as descriptive risk narrative. And the right-sided threshold is a completely different number: >20 mm. Don't mix them up.
Neurologic complications — when can you still operate? This is the question that paralyzes teams, and the answer is more permissive than most people think.
  • TIA → operate without delay if otherwise indicated. (Class I B)
  • Ischemic stroke → operate without any delay if there is heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess, or persistent high embolic risk — provided coma is absent and hemorrhage has been excluded on CT/MRI. (Class I B) Do not reflexively postpone surgery for a stroke.
  • Intracranial hemorrhage → delay surgery >1 month if the patient is stable. (Class IIa C)
  • ICH but unstable (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, high embolic risk) → urgent/emergency surgery should still be considered, weighing the chance of a meaningful neurologic outcome. (Class IIa C)
The embolic benefit of surgery is front-loaded: embolic risk falls steeply within the first two weeks of effective antibiotics. Operating in week four to "prevent a stroke" is largely closing the barn door.
Also non-negotiable: the hardware comes outIn CIED-related IE, the device and all leads must be completely removed — antibiotics alone will not clear a lead biofilm, and leaving it in means relapse.
Context

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🧩

How the company IE keeps changes your plan

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes management
CKD / dialysisDialysis access is a leading route to healthcare-associated S. aureus IE. Renal failure independently predicts death; HD-requiring AKI carries ~40% mortality.Renally dose vancomycin (target the AUC, not a trough) and daptomycin (extend to q48h if CrCl <30; dose after HD). Avoid gentamicin synergy if you can — and if enterococcal, this is precisely the patient for ampicillin + ceftriaxone. Favor hepatically-cleared agents (ceftriaxone, nafcillin).
Injection drug useRight-sided, tricuspid, S. aureus. Presents with septic pulmonary emboli, not stroke. Rising sharply; drives rising US IE mortality in the young.Start MOUD (buprenorphine/methadone) in hospital — it halves mortality and is the most effective thing you will do. Treat pain and withdrawal properly. Addiction medicine on the team from day one. Beware: rifampin induces methadone metabolism and can precipitate acute withdrawal.
Prosthetic valveHigher mortality; abscess in 56–100%; biofilm on an abiotic surface no antibiotic sterilizes.TEE up front — always. Add rifampin (only here) + gentamicin ×2 wk. ≥6 weeks of therapy. Expect surgery.
Heart failureThe most frequent complication (32%) and the #1 surgical indication.Acute severe regurgitation is a surgical problem, not a diuretic problem. Diuretics and afterload reduction are a bridge to the OR, not a destination.
Prior stroke / neuro eventSymptomatic in ~35%; silent lesions in 60–80%. Mycotic aneurysms rupture in ~36%.Image the brain. An ischemic stroke without coma or hemorrhage does not delay surgery; an ICH delays it >1 month. No thrombolysis (Class III).
Mechanical valve on warfarinThe anticoagulation question — and the answer is not a blanket "stop it."See the ICU panel. In brief: no stroke/bleed → continue anticoagulation; ICH → hold, then restart UFH ASAP after multidisciplinary discussion; surgery likely soon → switch to UFH. DOACs are not acceptable in mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN).
CirrhosisImpaired clearance of hepatically-metabolized antibiotics; higher bleeding/surgical risk.Nafcillin clearance falls substantially — consider adjustment. Cirrhosis is an explicit exclusion for OPAT — these patients stay inpatient.
HIV on ARTThe problem is drug interaction, not the HIV.Rifampin wrecks ART — it cuts protease-inhibitor levels >90%. Substitute rifabutin and co-manage with HIV pharmacy.
PregnancyRare but high-stakes; add obstetrics/neonatology to the team.β-lactams and vancomycin are the backbone. Avoid aminoglycosides (fetal oto/nephrotoxicity) and doxycycline (teeth/bone) — which makes the culture-negative regimens genuinely difficult. ID + MFM, always.
Drugs & practices to AVOID in infective endocarditis
  • Do not START anticoagulation or antiplatelets as "treatment" for IE. No proven benefit, and a real risk of hemorrhagic transformation of septic cerebral emboli. IE by itself is not an indication for antithrombotics.
  • No thrombolysis for IE-related embolic stroke (Class III) — the brain may be full of mycotic aneurysms.
  • No adjunctive gentamicin for native-valve staphylococcal IE — nephrotoxic, no benefit (Cosgrove, CID 2009).
  • No rifampin monotherapy — ever — and don't start rifampin before the bacteremia has cleared.
  • No rifampin for native-valve IE at all. It is for foreign material only.
  • No daptomycin for pneumonia — pulmonary surfactant inactivates it.
  • No penicillin/ampicillin for HACEK without proven susceptibility (Class III) — assume β-lactamase.
  • No vancomycin for MSSA once susceptibility is known — a β-lactam is clearly superior.
  • Avoid vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam together when cefepime would do — a well-documented AKI signal.
  • No DOACs in mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN: more clots and more bleeding).
  • Don't give antibiotics before blood cultures in a stable patient — you are manufacturing culture-negative IE. (But never delay antibiotics in sepsis.)
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Numeric triggers — don't hand-wave "looks unwell"

Transfer to the ICU — and urgently re-discuss with the Endocarditis Team — for any of:
  • Septic shock — vasopressors needed to hold MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume (Sepsis-3). Happens in 5–10% of IE.
  • Cardiogenic shock or refractory pulmonary edema from acute severe AR/MR → this is an emergency surgical indication (<24 h), not an ICU-management problem.
  • New complete (third-degree) AV block, or any high-grade block — needs pacing and means a root abscess.
  • Respiratory failure needing NIV or intubation — cardiogenic edema, or septic pulmonary emboli in right-sided IE.
  • Large embolic stroke, depressed consciousness, or a suspected mycotic aneurysm/ICH.
  • Persistent sepsis despite appropriate antibiotics — this is uncontrolled infection until proven otherwise.
ICU-admitted IE carries ~32% in-hospital mortality. Independent predictors of death: age, SAPS II, organ failure, stroke, and Staphylococcus. Notably, having cardiac surgery was associated with better survival — so an unstable patient is an argument for calling the surgeon sooner, not later.
Dispo

Discharge, OPAT & oral step-down

🏠

Getting them out — safely

ESC frames the course in two phases. The critical phase is roughly the first 10 days — inpatient, IV, when most complications and deaths occur, and when surgery (if needed) should happen. The continuation phase — beyond 10 days of therapy, and/or ≥7 days after surgery — is when a stable patient can move to OPAT or oral step-down.

Clinically stableAfebrile, hemodynamically stable, no uncontrolled heart failure.Required
Cultures clearedDocumented negative blood cultures.Required
No undrained focusNo abscess — cardiac or extracardiac (splenic, psoas, vertebral). Drain it first.Required
TEE before the switchClass I. A TEE must show no local progression and no complication before you go to OPAT or oral. This is not optional and it is frequently forgotten.Class I
≥10 days of IV therapyAnd ≥7 days post-surgery if they were operated on.Required
Follow-up in placeReliable access, home situation, and monitoring: nursing once daily, physician 1–3× per week. Weekly CBC + renal function; CRP q2–3 days until clearly falling.Required
POET partial-oral eligibility — can this patient finish by mouth?
Inclusion — ALL must be true
Left-sided IE (native or prosthetic)
Organism is streptococcus, E. faecalis, S. aureus, or CoNS
Received ≥10 days of IV antibiotics, with ≥10 days of treatment still remaining
Afebrile >2 days (temp <38 °C)
CRP <25% of peak, or <20 mg/L, and WBC <15 ×10⁹/L
TTE and TEE within 48 h confirming no surgical indication
No indication for cardiac surgery (or surgery already done)
Exclusion — ANY disqualifies
Abscess on TEE
BMI >40 kg/m²
Concomitant infection needing ongoing IV antibiotics
Suspected impaired GI absorption
Concern about adherence / unable to consent
NOT ELIGIBLE

If eligible, the switch is to two oral agents from different classes, chosen by organism and susceptibility, for the same total duration. Exact per-organism oral regimens should be set with ID — the POET protocol's dosing table is best read from the trial's own appendix rather than reproduced from memory.

Where do they go?

Home — oral

Meets POET criteria; reliable; TEE clear. Complete the course PO with close ID follow-up.

Home + OPAT

Stable, past the critical phase, PICC in place, safe home, daily nursing. The commonest path.

SNF

Needs ongoing IV therapy but is not independent enough for home OPAT.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-stroke or heavily deconditioned; can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged ventilator wean or complex sternotomy/wound care after valve surgery.

Palliative / hospice

Inoperable with a surgical indication, or recurrent IE with untreatable substance use and a poor prognosis — an honest, common, and often-avoided conversation.
OPAT in people who inject drugs — the guideline is more generous than the reflex. The AHA 2022 PWID statement does not treat injection drug use as an automatic OPAT disqualifier; it recommends assessing PWID against the same criteria as anyone else, and explicitly promotes integrated models — OPAT co-located with MOUD treatment, addiction-friendly residential programs, medical respite. The context matters: patient-directed (AMA) discharge among PWID with endocarditis ran as high as 21%. Reflexively keeping someone inpatient for six weeks without treating their pain, withdrawal and stigma does not produce a completed antibiotic course — it produces an empty bed and a relapse.
🫀 ICU — shock, the destroyed valve & the bleeding brain
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

Why IE lands in the unit — and it's almost never "just the infection"

Endocarditis patients come to the ICU for one of two fundamentally different reasons, and confusing them is dangerous:

PathwayDefinition / triggerWhat actually fixes it
Septic shock
5–10% of IE		Vasopressors required to hold MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume (Sepsis-3, as adopted by ESC)Antibiotics + source control. If the source is an abscess or an infected prosthesis, the "source control" is the surgeon.
Cardiogenic shock
acute valve destruction		Refractory pulmonary edema or shock from acute severe AR/MR, obstruction, or fistulaEMERGENCY SURGERY within 24 h (Class I B). Every drug below is a bridge to the operating room — nothing else fixes a destroyed valve.

Other ICU triggers: new complete heart block, respiratory failure (cardiogenic edema or septic pulmonary emboli), large embolic stroke or intracranial hemorrhage, and persistent sepsis despite appropriate antibiotics.

The single most important idea in this panel: acute severe regurgitation is a surgical disease with a very short fuse. The ventricle and atrium have had no time to dilate, so they are stiff and non-compliant — the regurgitant volume translates into a catastrophic pressure spike rather than a tolerated volume load. That is why a patient with acute severe AR can look fine and then be in florid pulmonary edema an hour later, and why "let's optimize them medically for a few days first" kills people. ICU-admitted IE carries ~32% in-hospital mortality — and in that cohort, having surgery was associated with better survival.

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, and what to trend

Arterial lineBeat-to-beat MAP for pressor titration. In acute severe AR you will see a wide pulse pressure with a low diastolic — and the low diastolic is what is starving the coronaries.Standard
Central accessFor vasopressors. Note the tension: a central line is another intravascular foreign body in a patient whose problem is an intravascular infection — remove it as soon as it isn't needed.Standard
Continuous telemetry + DAILY 12-leadThe PR interval. A lengthening PR = root abscess eating toward the AV node = urgent surgery. Do not let this be discovered by a code blue.Critical
Serial echoValve function, vegetation size, and new perivalvular extension. A patient deteriorating hemodynamically needs a repeat echo now, not tomorrow.Critical
Lactate + MAPThe shock targets: MAP ≥65, lactate clearing. Rising lactate on adequate pressors = failing pump or uncontrolled source.q2–6h
Creatinine + drug levelsAKI hits 40–69% of IE. Vancomycin AUC, gentamicin peak/trough, CK weekly on daptomycin.Daily
Blood culturesq24–48h until negative. >1 week of positive cultures = uncontrolled infection = surgical indication (IIa).Daily
Support

Pressors, inotropes & the destroyed valve

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick it
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β1 — vasoconstriction with modest inotropy0.01–3 mcg/kg/min, titrated to MAP ≥65↑↑ SVR, mild ↑ CO, minimal tachycardiaFirst-line for septic shock (Surviving Sepsis). Lower mortality and fewer arrhythmias than dopamine.
VasopressinV1 receptor — vasoconstriction by a non-catecholamine pathwayFixed 0.03 U/min — added, not titrated↑ SVR; catecholamine-sparingAdd when norepinephrine reaches ~0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min without hitting target — rather than pushing norepinephrine ever higher.
Epinephrineβ1/β2 at low dose → α1 dominant at high dose0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ CO and ↑ SVR; ↑ lactate (a β2 effect — don't misread it as worsening perfusion)Refractory shock, or when you need inotropy plus vasoconstriction together.
Dobutamineβ1 agonist (some β2) → ↑ cAMP → ↑ contractility2.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑↑ contractility, ↑ HR, ↓ SVR (can drop the BP)The inotrope for a failing pump with persistent hypoperfusion despite volume and pressors — and the one that fits the acute-AR physiology (see below).
Sodium nitroprussideNO donor → arterial & venous vasodilationTitrate to effect, per ICU protocol↓↓ afterload → more forward flow, less regurgitant flowThe vasodilator of choice for afterload reduction in acute severe regurgitation — if the blood pressure tolerates it.

Milrinone (a PDE-3 inhibitor "inodilator") is an alternative to dobutamine, but it is renally cleared and accumulates in AKI — which, given that 40–69% of IE patients develop renal failure, makes it a poor default here. Dose per your unit's protocol.

Acute severe AORTIC regurgitation — the physiology is counter-intuitive, and getting it wrong is lethal

DoWhy
Keep the heart rate FAST (high-normal)Regurgitation happens in diastole. A faster rate shortens diastole → less time to leak backwards → more forward output. This is why you must NOT give a beta-blocker. Slowing the heart lengthens diastole and increases the regurgitant volume — the intuitive move is the harmful one.
Reduce afterload (nitroprusside)Lower aortic impedance favors forward flow over backward flow across the incompetent valve.
Support contractility (dobutamine)Maintains forward stroke volume while you get to the OR.
Call the surgeonAll of the above is a bridge. Only valve replacement prevents the hemodynamic collapse.
An intra-aortic balloon pump is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in significant aortic regurgitation. The IABP inflates in diastole — precisely when the incompetent aortic valve is leaking. Raising the diastolic aortic pressure drives more blood backwards through the regurgitant valve, worsening the very lesion you are trying to support. This is a genuine never-event.

Note the contrast with acute severe MITRAL regurgitation: there, an IABP is useful — afterload reduction lowers the regurgitant fraction across the mitral valve, and diastolic augmentation does not worsen mitral backflow the way it worsens aortic backflow. Same device, opposite answer, depending on which valve broke. Know which valve you are dealing with before anyone floats a balloon.
Airway

Respiratory support & ventilator

🌬️

Two different lungs, two different strategies

① Cardiogenic pulmonary edema — from the destroyed left-sided valve

NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) first, if the patient can protect their airway and is not in florid shock. Positive pressure reduces preload and afterload and recruits flooded alveoli. Intubate for NIV failure, exhaustion, depressed consciousness, or shock. Remember that the definitive treatment is the operating room — do not let a comfortable BiPAP mask become a reason to delay surgery.

② Septic pulmonary emboli / ARDS — from right-sided IE

Lung-protective ventilation, per ARDSNet:

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg PBW
down to 4 if needed for pressures
Plateau pressure
≤30 cmH₂O
the number that matters
PEEP / FiO₂
ARDSNet table
titrate together
SpO₂ target
88–95%
don't chase 100%

ARDSNet (NEJM 2000) reduced mortality from 39.8% → 31.0% with 6 mL/kg vs 12 mL/kg. Not an IE-specific trial — but this is the lung you are ventilating.

Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — but that does NOT rule it out in right-sided IE. The distinction is anatomical: surfactant lives in the alveolus. Septic pulmonary emboli are an intravascular, embolic phenomenon — the drug never has to work inside an alveolus. So daptomycin remains effective for the endocarditis that is showering the lungs. What you must not do is use daptomycin to treat an actual pneumonia. Precision about the compartment is the whole point.
Rescue

Neuro complications & anticoagulation

🧠

The hardest calls in the disease

Complete heart block

Temporary pacing (transvenous — or epicardial if they are already in the operating room). But the block is a symptom: it means the abscess has reached the conduction system, and that is a Class I urgent surgical indication. Pacing buys time; it does not treat the disease. ESC identifies five predictors of persistent AV block that should prompt immediate epicardial pacemaker implantation at the time of valve surgery (Class IIa): pre-operative conduction abnormality · S. aureus · aortic root abscess · tricuspid involvement · previous valve surgery.

Embolic stroke, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage

  • Silent lesions are the norm — brain MRI finds them in 60–80%. Symptomatic cerebrovascular events occur in ~35%.
  • Mycotic (infective) aneurysms rupture in ~36%. Get CT/MR angiography in any IE patient with neurologic symptoms (Class I B). "Mycotic" means mushroom-shaped, not fungal.
  • Thrombolysis is NOT recommended in IE-related embolic stroke (Class III) — the brain may be seeded with mycotic aneurysms, and you will convert an infarct into a hemorrhage.
  • Mechanical thrombectomy may be considered for large-vessel occlusion within the appropriate window (Class IIb C).
Anticoagulation in IE — the question you will be asked, and the answer is stratified, not binary.
SituationWhat ESC 2023 actually saysClass
IE, no other indicationIE by itself is NOT an indication for antithrombotics or anticoagulants. Do not start them.—
Pre-existing indication (e.g. mechanical valve), no stroke, no bleedCONTINUE the anticoagulation. It did not raise stroke, cerebral hemorrhage, or 10-week mortality in left-sided IE. The reflex to stop it is not evidence-based.—
Major bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhageINTERRUPT antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy.I C
ICH + mechanical valveRestart unfractionated heparin as soon as possible, after multidisciplinary discussion. (You cannot leave a mechanical valve un-anticoagulated indefinitely.)IIa C
No stroke, but surgery likely soon (e.g. S. aureus IE)Replace the oral anticoagulant with UFH, closely monitored — it is short-acting and reversible.IIa C
ThrombolysisNOT recommended.III C
ESC is candid that the level of evidence here is low — nearly everything is Level C. Every one of these decisions belongs to the Endocarditis Team, not to a lone overnight resident. And DOACs are never an acceptable substitute for warfarin in a mechanical valve (RE-ALIGN was stopped early for more clotting and more bleeding).
Downgrade

When to step down

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Ready for the floor when ALL of:
  • Off vasopressors ≥6–12 h with a stable MAP ≥65 and no escalating support.
  • Lactate normalized (<2 mmol/L) and trending down.
  • Extubated and stable on room air or low-flow O₂ (or at a stable, sustainable baseline).
  • No high-grade AV block — or a stable underlying rhythm if paced.
  • Blood cultures clearing on appropriate targeted antibiotics.
  • Any surgical indication has been addressed — operated on, or an explicit, documented Endocarditis Team decision not to operate.
NOT yet, even if the numbers look good, if: there is an unaddressed surgical indication (an abscess does not resolve on antibiotics — it is a bomb on a timer) · blood cultures are still positive · the PR interval is lengthening · there is a new murmur or falling blood pressure · or an untreated mycotic aneurysm. Hemodynamic stability in a patient with an untreated root abscess is not stability — it is the calm before the block.

Note honestly: no IE-specific numeric downgrade criteria exist in ESC 2023 — the thresholds above are standard critical-care practice, with the IE-specific additions (cultures, PR interval, surgical indication) layered on top. Say that out loud rather than pretending a guideline number exists.

Goals of care

Two conversations get avoided far too long in this disease, and both belong to you: ① the patient with a clear surgical indication who is not a surgical candidate — their prognosis is poor and they deserve to know it; ② the patient with recurrent IE and untreated substance use disorder, sometimes facing a second or third valve. The answer is not to quietly write them off — it is to treat the addiction as aggressively as you treat the infection, and to be honest about prognosis if that is not possible. Involve palliative care early; it is not giving up.

Refs

Sources, trials & media

Guidelines & primary criteria

  • 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis (Delgado V, Ajmone Marsan N, et al. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042) — the current comprehensive management guideline, and the first ESC update in 8 years. Eur Heart J · DOI · PubMed. (A Correction was published — Eur Heart J 2025;46:1082 — an errata notice, not a new focused update.)
  • 2023 Duke-ISCVID Criteria for Infective Endocarditis (Fowler VG Jr, Durack DT, Selton-Suty C, et al. Clin Infect Dis 2023;77:518–526) — CID · DOI · MDCalc version
  • AHA 2015 Scientific Statement — Infective Endocarditis in Adults (Baddour LM, et al. Circulation 2015;132:1435–1486; endorsed by IDSA) — still the principal US antimicrobial-dosing reference. AHA has issued no newer comprehensive management statement. Circulation · Full PDF (IDSA)
  • AHA 2021 — Prevention of Viridans Group Streptococcal IE (Wilson WR, et al. Circulation 2021;143:e963–e978) — the current prophylaxis statement; the one that removed clindamycin. Circulation
  • AHA 2022 — Management of IE in People Who Inject Drugs (Baddour LM, et al. Circulation 2022;146:e187–e201) — Circulation
  • AHA 2023 Science Advisory — Nondental Invasive Procedures and Risk of IE (Circulation 2023;148:1529–1541) — Circulation
  • AHA 2025 Scientific Statement — Blood Culture–Negative Endocarditis (DeSimone DC, et al. J Am Heart Assoc 2025;14:e040218) — JAHA
  • 2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP Vancomycin Therapeutic Monitoring Consensus (Rybak MJ, et al.) — the source of the AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 target. Full PDF

Validated scores — built in here, or deliberately linked out

  • Built into this page: the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria · VIRSTA (echo triage in S. aureus bacteremia) · POET partial-oral eligibility · the IE antibiotic-prophylaxis decision tool.
  • VIRSTA score — Tubiana S, et al. J Infect 2016;72:544–553. The score ESC 2023 itself cites for echo triage in SAB.
  • PREDICT score — Palraj BR, et al. Clin Infect Dis 2015;61:18–28. Day-5 score <2 → TEE can reasonably be deferred. (No MDCalc page exists — use the primary paper.)
  • DENOVA score — Berge A, et al. Infection 2019;47:45–50. Echo triage in monomicrobial E. faecalis bacteremia; ≥3 → get the echo. Shown above as a reference table rather than reimplemented as a live calculator, because the exact point table could only be confirmed from a secondary reprint of the original.
  • Embolic Risk (ER) French score — Hubert S, et al. JACC 2013;62:1384–1392; this is the embolic-risk calculator ESC 2023 alludes to. It is a Cox proportional-hazards model, not an additive point score, so it is deliberately not reimplemented here — run it on the validated tool. ebmcalc

Key trials

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
POET2019Partial oral step-down vs continued IV in stabilized left-sided IE: composite 9.0% vs 12.1% — non-inferior (OR 0.72).Broke the dogma that IE always means 4–6 weeks of IV. Underpins the oral step-down pathway — after ≥10 days IV, stability, and a clean TEE.
POET 5-year2022At median 5.4 y: composite 32.8% (oral) vs 45.2% (IV), HR 0.65; mortality 23.4% vs 35.2%.Answered the obvious worry — no late relapse with oral therapy. If anything the oral arm did better. Made oral step-down credible.
EASE2012Early surgery (<48 h) vs conventional care in left-sided IE with severe valve disease + vegetation >10 mm: death/embolism 3% vs 23% (HR 0.10). Embolic events at 6 mo: 0% vs 21%.The RCT behind "operate on the big vegetation." Embolic events collapse with early surgery — no mortality penalty. Underpins the ESC ≥10 mm rules.
ARREST2018Adjunctive rifampicin in S. aureus bacteremia (n=758): failure/recurrence/death 17% vs 18%, HR 0.96 — no benefit. More adverse events (17% vs 10%) and drug interactions.Killed enthusiasm for routine rifampin add-on. Rifampin's place is foreign material only — not native-valve disease, not bacteremia generally.
CAMERA22020Adding an antistaphylococcal β-lactam to vanc/dapto for MRSA bacteremia: composite 35% vs 39% (ns) — but AKI 23% vs 6%. Stopped early by the DSMB for harm.The definitive "faster bacteremia clearance ≠ better outcomes" lesson. Combination therapy bought a microbiologic surrogate and paid for it in kidneys.
Fowler — daptomycin2006Daptomycin 6 mg/kg vs standard therapy (+ low-dose gent) for S. aureus bacteremia/right-sided IE: success 44.2% vs 41.7% — non-inferior.Put daptomycin on the map as a once-daily alternative to vancomycin — and set up the nephrotoxicity analysis that followed.
Cosgrove — gentamicin2009Initial low-dose adjunctive gentamicin: fall in creatinine clearance in 22% vs 8% (P=.005) — with no efficacy benefit.Why we no longer add gentamicin for native-valve staphylococcal IE. Pure toxicity, zero gain. Cited by both AHA and ESC.
Fernández-Hidalgo2013Ampicillin + ceftriaxone vs ampicillin + gentamicin for E. faecalis IE (n=246): equivalent mortality and relapse — but new renal failure 23% (amp+gent) vs 0% (amp+CTX).The dual-β-lactam regimen. Equal efficacy, no nephrotoxicity, and it still works with HLAR — which is why it has displaced amp+gent.
DOTS — dalbavancin2025Two-dose dalbavancin (1500 mg day 1 + day 8) vs 4–8 weeks of standard IV for complicated S. aureus bacteremia (n=200): DOOR 47.7% — not superior, but clinical success 73% vs 72% met non-inferiority.The newest entry: a long-acting lipoglycopeptide that could replace weeks of IV access. But note — DOTS explicitly EXCLUDED left-sided IE. Do not extrapolate it to native/prosthetic left-sided disease.

Educational reference for an incoming IM resident. Every dose, threshold and percentage on this page traces to the primary guideline, trial or registry cited above. Verify against your institution's formulary and the current guideline before acting on any individual patient. Class-of-recommendation labels (I / IIa / IIb) are those of the 2023 ESC endocarditis guideline. Where ESC 2023 and the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria genuinely disagree, both positions are shown rather than silently reconciled.
